problem: The example is backwards. When a C function returns, the local's name is not in scope anywhere in the caller — the caller cannot write that name at all. What survives is the pointer and the dead storage, not a visible name. As written the sentence teaches a false picture of scope.
fix: Scope and lifetime are independent. A C function that returns the address of its local ends the lifetime of that storage when its record is popped, while the pointer in the caller is still in scope and now dangles. In the other direction, an inner block's storage may still exist after its name has gone out of scope. Text controls the name; the run controls the storage.

problem: 'A name can be in scope after its activation has returned' is wrong. Once the activation returns, its local names are no longer visible in the text at all, so they are out of scope as well as dead.
fix: Two names is in scope but its storage does not exist yet (a block not yet entered), and storage can exist or linger while a pointer to it is in scope after the name itself is out of scope. Scope is text, lifetime is the run; do not say a name stays in scope after its activation returns.

problem: 'The name stays in scope at the caller' is false — the local's name is not visible in the caller. The undefined behaviour comes from the dangling pointer and the reused record, which the rest of the answer already says correctly.
fix: The lifetime of the local's storage ends when the call returns and the record is popped. The caller's pointer is in scope but now points at storage that no longer belongs to that variable and may be reused by the next call, so dereferencing it is undefined.

problem: 'computes the address without knowing which activation is running' can be read as: the address does not depend on the running activation. It does. What is fixed at compile time is the distance, not the address.
fix: The compiler stores the distance as a pair (nesting depth, offset) and emits code that starts from the running activation's record and follows that many access links to reach the frame holding the declaration. The distance is static; the address is computed at run time with no search of the stack.

problem: 'A procedure ... takes parameters, does work and returns a result' excludes procedures that return nothing (void in C, a Fortran subroutine), which the same paragraph lists as procedures.
fix: A procedure is a named piece of code that takes parameters and does work on behalf of its caller; it may or may not return a result.
